CUSTOMER JOURNEY STORY INSTRUCTIONS
Last updated: April 2026 (Summit 2026 rebuild)
Retrieve this file before writing any customer journey story.
Also retrieve 04_pain_points.md for the relevant industry before writing.
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CORE PHILOSOPHY
Customer journey stories are told entirely from the perspective of a real person living their life. The brand responds intelligently to their moments, needs, and behaviours — but Adobe technology is never named or visible in the narrative. These stories show what a great experience feels like from the inside, and are used to inspire customers and prospects with what is possible.

The customer is always the hero. The brand is the enabler. Adobe is invisible.

This rule is unchanged post-Summit 2026. None of the Summit announcements (Adobe CX Enterprise, Coworker, Brand Intelligence, AI Collaborators, Marketing Agent in third-party AI surfaces, etc.) appear in the customer narrative layer of these stories. The post-Summit themes (Customer Engagement, Brand Visibility, Content Supply Chain) inform what gets emphasised in the story, but no Summit product names appear in the customer's experience.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SUMMIT 2026 — WHAT CHANGES, WHAT DOESN'T
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

WHAT CHANGES POST-SUMMIT:
— Theme inference applies. Read the brief and identify which Summit theme(s) the story expresses (Customer Engagement, Brand Visibility, Content Supply Chain). Themes shape what gets emphasised in the customer experience and what the orchestration layer references.
— The orchestration layer (visible to the consultant, not in the story) uses post-Summit product vocabulary: Adobe CX Enterprise as the surface, agents named, Coworker referenced if the underlying experience would have been Coworker-orchestrated, etc.
— New AI-mediated discovery moments may appear in the customer narrative — a customer first encountering the brand through ChatGPT or Gemini, asking a question and getting an accurate brand answer, then arriving at the brand site with context already established. The customer experiences this as a great answer; Adobe (LLM Optimizer, Brand Concierge) makes it possible underneath.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE:
— Adobe is invisible in the customer narrative. No Adobe product names. No "Coworker," no "Brand Intelligence," no "Brand Concierge" in the customer's mouth or the narrator's voice when describing the customer's experience.
— The story structure (Persona Card, Scene-by-Scene, Orchestration Layer, Adobe Products Powering This Experience) is unchanged.
— The persona card format is unchanged.
— The scene structure is unchanged.
— Channel behaviour guidelines are unchanged.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
BEFORE WRITING — WHAT TO COLLECT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Before writing, confirm or assume:
1. Brand and industry
2. Customer persona — name, age, life situation, personal goal or tension
3. Life moment or trigger — the occasion, goal, or event driving the story
4. Channels in scope — or say "all relevant" and decide based on context
5. Single customer or multiple personas

If minimal input is given, state assumptions and confirm before proceeding. Retrieve 04_pain_points.md for the relevant industry to ground the story in real frustrations.

The default-first behaviour and two-mode system from marketer story instructions does NOT apply to customer journey stories. Customer journey stories continue to use the existing intake approach (state assumptions, confirm before proceeding) because the modes are about how Adobe technology is shown — and Adobe is invisible in customer journey stories anyway.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THEME INFERENCE — APPLIES TO CUSTOMER JOURNEY STORIES TOO
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Read the brief and identify which Summit 2026 theme(s) the story expresses:

CUSTOMER ENGAGEMENT — when the story is primarily about the customer feeling known, having a journey that responds to them in real time, receiving relevant offers, building loyalty through the experience itself.

BRAND VISIBILITY — when the story includes a moment where the customer first encounters the brand through an AI surface (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, voice assistant), or where the brand shows up accurately in an AI-mediated discovery moment.

CONTENT SUPPLY CHAIN — when the story is primarily about the content the customer receives feeling consistently on-brand and relevant, even when scaled across many touchpoints.

The theme(s) shape the orchestration layer (which Adobe products are referenced as powering the experience) but never appear in the customer narrative itself. A customer doesn't say "wow, the brand has great content supply chain" — they say "wow, every email actually feels written for me."

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
PERSONA CARD — PRODUCE AT THE START OF EVERY STORY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

NAME:
AGE:
LOCATION:
LIFE SITUATION: [1–2 sentences — who they are and how they live]
PERSONAL GOAL: [What they are trying to achieve — the driving motivation of this story]
RELATIONSHIP WITH BRAND: [How long they have been a customer, how they typically engage, any notable behaviours or history]
CHANNEL PREFERENCES: [How they prefer to be reached and which devices they use]
STARTING SEGMENTS: [2–4 audience segments they are already in at the start of the story — use specific names, not generic labels]
CHURN / RISK SIGNAL: [Any commercial tension at the start — declining spend, lapsing behaviour, unmet need — if applicable]

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SCENE STRUCTURE — MANDATORY FORMAT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Every scene follows this exact format. Do not skip any field.

SCENE HEADING
An evocative label from the customer's perspective — not the brand's.
Good: "Visa Reminder", "A Healthier Week", "The Flight Is Delayed", "Something She Didn't Ask For"
Bad: "Push Notification Sent", "Journey Triggered", "Re-engagement Campaign"

NARRATIVE
2–4 sentences. Third person, present tense. Technology is completely invisible. The brand's response should feel like good service — natural, timely, and helpful. Never mechanical or surveillance-like.

CHANNEL AND TOUCHPOINT
What channel this moment happens on. What the specific interaction looks like. Include the actual message content — notification text, email subject line, in-app message, chat dialogue — written exactly as the customer would see it. Never use placeholder copy.

PROFILE PANEL UPDATE
Shows the data layer building in real time. Always include this — it is the structural device that makes the technology visible to the sales audience watching the story, even though it never appears in the narrative itself.

Format:
EXPERIENCE EVENTS (new this scene):
— [event type]: [specific detail]
— [event type]: [specific detail]

SEGMENTS UPDATED:
— Added: [segment name — specific, not generic]
— Added: [segment name]

IDENTITIES (if a new ID is resolved this scene):
— [identity type]: [value or description]

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
TIME DIMENSION — MANDATORY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Every story must include time markers that show the arc. The profile panel should show events accumulating and segments updating progressively across scenes. This is critical — it shows the value of the real-time profile building up over time.

Time marker examples:
— "Two weeks before the trip..."
— "The following Sunday morning..."
— "Three months later, after moving back to Dubai..."
— "On the morning of the flight..."
— "That evening, scrolling through TikTok..."

The arc should cover at minimum two distinct time periods. Long stories can span weeks or months.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHANNEL BEHAVIOUR GUIDELINES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PUSH NOTIFICATIONS
Short, personal, action-oriented. Always tied to a real signal — location, time, behaviour, event. Maximum 2 lines. Include the sender name and a timestamp if shown on a lock screen. Never send without a clear trigger.

EMAIL
Used for richer content: education, programme enrolment, longer consideration moments, post-purchase follow-up. Always include a subject line and the key message or content of the email. Not every interaction should be an offer — service and educational emails are as important as promotional ones.

SMS / WHATSAPP
Transactional and time-sensitive. Delivery updates, reminders, urgent offers. Always short. Only send when the customer has given explicit consent for that channel.

IN-APP
The richest channel. Reflects the customer's full profile. Can include personalised homepage content, local offers, shopping lists, programme progress, conversational AI interactions. Show actual dialogue where relevant — not "user sees recommendations" but what the specific recommendations are and what the customer says or does.

IN-STORE / PHYSICAL
Scanner interactions, till moments, location-based triggers, smart mirror or kiosk experiences. This is where digital and physical knowledge of the customer converge — the most powerful moments often happen here. Show it feeling natural, not intrusive.

PAID MEDIA
Social Media websites, news outlets, recipe websites. This is where a customer gets exposed to the messaging of the brand. Normally used in customer acquisition. Keep it as a flow and linked to the narrative and relevant to the persona activity and story.

BRAND CONCIERGE (CUSTOMER-FACING)
Natural dialogue that guides, suggests, and assists. Never pushy. Never scripted-sounding. The customer should feel like they are talking to someone who knows them and is genuinely trying to help. Always include actual dialogue — not a description of dialogue. Show the customer making a choice, not just receiving information. Never name "Brand Concierge" in the customer narrative — it appears as a helpful, knowledgeable conversational interface on the brand's website or app.

AI-MEDIATED DISCOVERY (POST-SUMMIT 2026 ADDITION)
A new channel pattern: the customer first encounters the brand through a third-party AI surface (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, voice assistant, AI-driven search). They ask a question — get a brand answer that's accurate, helpful, and trustworthy. Often they take action directly inside the AI surface (a recommendation, a comparison, a cart add) before ever visiting the brand's site.
Show:
— The customer asking a real question, in their words
— The AI surface returning a useful answer that mentions or shows the brand correctly
— The customer making a choice within that environment, or arriving at the brand site with intent already formed
Never name the underlying technology (LLM Optimizer, Brand Concierge integrations, Adobe Commerce) — the customer just experiences a great answer. The orchestration layer references the products that made it possible.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SCENE PATTERNS — USE THESE TO BUILD THE STORY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Draw from these patterns to create a varied and compelling arc:

THE PROACTIVE HELPFUL NUDGE
The brand anticipates a need before the customer asks. Faisal receives a visa reminder two weeks before his trip. Hannah is told she's spent £10 on delivery charges this month and would save with a delivery saver plan. The customer thinks: "How did they know I needed that?"

THE MOMENT OF RECOGNITION
The customer feels known. Their bags are already checked in when they arrive at the airport. Their usual order is pre-loaded when they open the app on a Sunday. They don't have to explain themselves.

THE PREFERENCE SIGNAL
The customer takes an action that enriches their profile — choosing favourite brands, adding to a shopping list, completing a health programme check-in. The brand responds by personalising the experience further. The customer feels in control, not tracked.

THE UNEXPECTED DELIGHT
Something that goes beyond the transaction. The children's airport artwork continues on the inflight entertainment screen. The recipe suggestion arrives with a Whoosh delivery option because the ingredient is missing from the fridge. The customer didn't ask for it but immediately values it.

THE FRICTION RESOLVED
A pain point removed in real time. The security queue is long — fast track is offered. The delivery slot has a cut-off in 20 minutes — the app reminds them in time. The customer's usual product is on offer at the local store — they're notified as they walk past. The relief is tangible.

THE COMMERCIAL MOMENT DONE WELL
An upsell or cross-sell that feels relevant and timely, not opportunistic. The offer comes at exactly the right moment — when the customer has demonstrated intent, not just proximity. John's cabin upgrade option appears after he has already committed to the cruise. Amina's Manchester City bundle arrives during the flight, not before.

THE LIFECYCLE SIGNAL
A behaviour pattern that triggers a journey. Hannah's weekly spend has been declining for two months — the brand responds with inspiration content, not a discount. Amina has never enrolled in the loyalty programme despite flying frequently — she is gently invited at the right moment.

THE AI DISCOVERY MOMENT (POST-SUMMIT 2026)
The customer first encounters the brand through an AI surface. They ask a research question, receive a brand-aware answer, take a small action (compare, save, sign up for a free trial), then arrive at the brand site with context already in place. By the time the brand "sees" them, the conversation has already started.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SEGMENT NAMING CONVENTION
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Always use specific, realistic segment names. Never use generic labels.

Good examples:
— "Well-being focused — Vegetarian"
— "Delivery Saver Prospect"
— "Spend Decline — 2 Month Trend"
— "F&F Activewear High Propensity"
— "Family Traveller — Multi-Generational"
— "Ramadan Offer Interest"
— "FlexDirect Target Audience"
— "Whoosh Acquisition — Top 10% Propensity"
— "LLM Referrer — Wellbeing Segment"
— "AI Search — Mascara Trend Cohort" (post-Summit AI-mediated discovery example)

Bad examples:
— "High Value Customer"
— "Engaged User"
— "At Risk"
— "Segment A"

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NARRATIVE RULES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

— Always write in third person, present tense: "Hannah opens the app and sees..."
— The customer must feel like a real person — give them texture, habits, contradictions, a life outside the brand
— The brand's intelligence should feel like good service, not surveillance — consent has been given, data is used to help
— Each touchpoint must be earned — the brand responds to something the customer has actually done or signalled
— Include at least one moment of genuine delight — something the customer didn't expect but appreciated
— Include at least one moment of friction that the brand resolves — this makes the technology feel useful
— End the story with a clear human outcome: a goal achieved, a relationship strengthened, a habit formed, a decision made
— The customer makes choices throughout — they are never passive
— Adobe never appears in the customer narrative — no product names, no "Coworker," no "Brand Concierge," no "AI Assistant"

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VARIATION GUIDANCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

When producing multiple customer journey stories, deliberately vary:
— Life stage: student, young professional, parent, retiree, recent mover
— Cultural and geographic context: the Faisal story is set in Saudi Arabia with Ramadan as the occasion — this specificity matters enormously
— Primary commercial tension: acquisition, retention, churn prevention, upsell, cross-sell into a new proposition
— The hero channel: rotate which channel carries the most weight in the story — including AI-mediated discovery as a possible hero channel post-Summit
— Emotional tone: excitement, reassurance, discovery, belonging, relief — not every story has the same register
— Arc length: some stories span a single day, others span weeks or months
— Summit theme expressed: rotate Customer Engagement, Brand Visibility, Content Supply Chain primary themes

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OUTPUT FORMAT — FOUR SECTIONS (UNCHANGED)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. PERSONA CARD
Following the format above.

B. THE STORY
Scene by scene — heading, narrative, channel and touchpoint, profile panel update. Time markers between scenes where the arc jumps forward.

C. ORCHESTRATION LAYER
This section is for the sales audience — it maps the technology powering each story moment. For each scene, include:
— Signal or trigger: what data event or behaviour triggered this moment
— Adobe product: which product powers this moment (named explicitly here — not in the narrative). Use post-Summit product names: Adobe CX Enterprise as surface, AJO with new Summit skills, RTCDP with Re-imagined Audiences, Brand Intelligence for governance, Brand Concierge with new integrations, LLM Optimizer for AI discovery moments, etc.
— Business value: the KPI or outcome this moment drives
— Summit 2026 theme(s) expressed: which of the three pillars this moment supports

D. ADOBE PRODUCTS POWERING THIS EXPERIENCE
A clearly separated section listing every Adobe product that powered the story. For each: one sentence describing its specific role in this story. Never generic — always specific to what it did here.

Format:
[Product name] — [Specific role in this story]

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
WHAT NOT TO DO
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

— Never name Adobe products inside the customer narrative — including any post-Summit product names (Adobe CX Enterprise, Coworker, Brand Intelligence, etc.)
— Never make the data layer feel surveillance-like — the customer has consented
— Never write a touchpoint that is not grounded in something the customer has actually done or signalled
— Never make every interaction an offer or promotion — service moments are as important
— Never skip the profile panel — it is the structural device that shows the technology working
— Never make the customer passive — they make choices and feel in control throughout
— Never use placeholder copy — all message text must be exact words
— Never write all scenes with the same emotional tone — vary the register across the arc
— Never feature Coworker in customer journey stories — Coworker is for marketer stories only
— Never describe the AI surface (e.g. ChatGPT, Gemini) as Adobe — name the third-party surface honestly; the orchestration layer notes that LLM Optimizer made the brand show up correctly
